How kettles whistle

By Ada Fixture

A kettle whistles because steam is forced through two small holes in the spout cap. Between the holes the jet becomes unstable and sheds little vortices, and those vortices make the sound.

The pitch rises as the water boils harder. Researchers in Cambridge measured it in 2013 and found two regimes: a low flute-like note first, then the familiar shriek.

What you can try at home

  • Fill the kettle half way and listen for the first low note.
  • Lift the cap slightly: the whistle stops, because the jet no longer hits the second hole.
